served.stem: An intestinal cell is treated with a drug that completely blocks the sodium potassium ATPase. Within minutes, glucose uptake across the apical membrane by the sodium glucose cotransporter falls off sharply. What is the best explanation?
choices: The sodium gradient that powers the cotransporter runs down
The cotransporter needs ATP, and the drug has cut off its supply
The apical membrane depolarizes, which closes the carrier
The drug binds the glucose carrier directly and jams its binding site
Glucose is no longer phosphorylated once it arrives inside the cell
served.bankWhy: The real question is what secondary active transport runs on. The cotransporter never touches ATP: it lets sodium fall downhill and drags glucose uphill with it, and that sodium gradient is built by the pump. Block the pump, sodium piles up inside, the gradient flattens, and the free ride ends. Any time a transporter is labeled secondary active, look upstream for the pump that stocked its gradient.

answer.text: The sodium gradient that powers the cotransporter runs down
answer.line: The cotransporter runs on the sodium gradient the pump builds. Block the pump and the gradient drains, so glucose uptake fades.

steps: Trace the energy. The Na+/K+ pump spends ATP to keep sodium low inside the cell.
The cotransporter lets sodium run down that gradient and drags glucose in with it, uphill. It never touches ATP itself.
Block the pump and sodium leaks in until the gradient is gone. That takes minutes, which is why uptake falls off then.

choices.text: The sodium gradient that powers the cotransporter runs down
choices.note: No pump, no gradient, no free ride for glucose.

choices.text: The cotransporter needs ATP, and the drug has cut off its supply
choices.note: ATP powers the pump, primary active transport. The cotransporter never hydrolyzes ATP; it runs on the gradient.

choices.text: The apical membrane depolarizes, which closes the carrier
choices.note: Some depolarization does happen and trims the driving force. But the carrier does not close; losing the sodium gradient is the main cause.

choices.text: The drug binds the glucose carrier directly and jams its binding site
choices.note: The stem says the drug blocks the pump. A delay of minutes fits a gradient running down, not a direct block of the carrier.

choices.text: Glucose is no longer phosphorylated once it arrives inside the cell
choices.note: Hexokinase traps glucose in many cells by phosphorylating it. That is not the energy source for this carrier.

visual.alt: An intestinal cell between the gut lumen above and the blood below. In the top membrane the sodium glucose cotransporter lets Na+ run in and drags glucose with it; in the bottom membrane the Na+/K+ pump, crossed out by the drug, no longer sends Na+ out. Inside, Na+ builds up and the gradient runs down, outlined as the answer.
visual.caption: Find the crossed-out pump, then look up. The carrier above ran on the gradient that pump kept.
